summary: Iran weighs a two-day Hormuz plan as US strike talk grows, Oleshky evacuees reach Ukraine, US voters turn out early, Israel's deadlock deepens and a UN nature summit ends.

topics.heading: Iran and Qatar discuss a two-day plan to reopen Hormuz as US strike warnings grow
topics.summary: Iranian negotiators met Qatari mediators in Doha on Saturday after Iran found Qatar's seven-day plan unsatisfactory. Iran's foreign minister says a plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days is being discussed, while Gulf states expect possible US strikes after Tuesday's US election.[^1][^2]

lead.title: Iranian envoys meet Qatar mediators as US strike threat looms post-midterms

alsoReported.title: Araghchi says Vance's letter 'positive step' toward opening dialogue between Iran, US
Oman rescues 25 sailors from burning ship as Iran says tankers halted in Hormuz

article: Talks to end the US-Iran war moved on two tracks this weekend. Iranian and Qatari officials talked in Tehran for more than 12 hours on Friday, and Iranian negotiators met Qatar's mediators in Doha on Saturday; Reuters says the talks were coordinated with Washington[^1]. Iran did not accept Qatar's draft, a seven-day plan of daily trust-building steps before wider talks, but did not walk away either[^1]. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says a plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days is now under discussion, if the US cooperates[^2].

Iran has set conditions. According to the Jerusalem Post, Araghchi listed lifting recent sanctions, fewer US forces in the region, restored oil waivers and the release of frozen Iranian money, and he ruled out meeting US officials himself[^5]. Tehran says the US "tone has completely changed" since a letter from Vice-President JD Vance; President Trump says the letter was only about letting medical supplies into Iran[^4][^1]. Trump says the talks are "going fine" but that he is "not in that much of a hurry"[^2].

Meanwhile the strait stays dangerous. Iran's Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) say three tankers on an "unauthorized route" were halted after incidents or mine strikes; Oman's navy rescued 25 sailors from the burning tanker RITI[^3]. The US military's regional commander, Adm. Brad Cooper, says the main shipping lanes have been cleared of Iranian mines[^3].

What could come next is unclear. Secretary of State Marco Rubio says Trump has not decided on new strikes and prefers diplomacy, while countries in the region expect attacks could resume after the US midterm election on November 3[^1]. The Times of Israel reports that Gulf allies were warned strikes could come as early as November 4; neither government has confirmed it[^4]. Iran's Supreme Leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, has told the armed forces to prepare to respond to any attack[^1]. My read: the next week, with the US vote and any reply on the two-day plan, could decide whether this turns toward a deal or a new round of fighting.
topics.differences: Iran's IRGC says several tankers were stopped or hit mines; the US military says the main lanes are clear[^3]. On Vance's letter, Tehran describes a changed US tone, while Trump says it only covered medical supplies[^4][^1]. Reports of planned strikes after the vote come from unnamed officials and are not confirmed[^1][^4].

topics.heading: Hundreds evacuated from occupied Oleshky reach Ukraine under a rare local truce
topics.summary: Residents of the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky crossed into Ukrainian-held territory on Saturday after a long route through Russia and Belarus. The local truce, which the White House says Melania Trump brokered, was due to end on Sunday evening.[^6][^8]

lead.title: Residents evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky reach Ukraine after localized ceasefire

alsoReported.title: Oleshky residents reach Ukrainian-controlled territory after escaping Russian occupation
Hundreds from Russian-occupied Oleshky land in Belarus en route to Ukraine

article: On Saturday, people evacuated from Oleshky, a town in Ukraine's Kherson region held by Russia since 2022, reached Ukrainian-controlled territory[^6][^7]. Their route was long: buses left on Friday for Anapa in southern Russia, four planes then flew them to Gomel in Belarus, and from there they crossed into Ukraine[^6][^8]. Residents could choose to go to Ukraine, go to Russia through Crimea, or stay with fresh supplies[^6].

Exact numbers are not public. About 750 people registered, and Kyiv withheld the final figures for security reasons[^6][^7]. About 2,000 people were still living in a town that had about 24,000 before the war[^7]. The White House says Melania Trump brokered the local truce, which began early on Tuesday and was expected to last until Sunday evening[^8][^6]. Ukraine's human-rights commissioner, Dmytro Lubinets, called it the longest pause in fighting anywhere along the front since 2022[^7].

The two sides tell the story differently. A Ukrainian volunteer and an unnamed source told the Kyiv Independent that Russia moved some people before the agreed start and tried to limit departures[^9][^7]. Russia's human-rights commissioner presented the operation as humanitarian and said some residents chose Russia[^8].

The truce was local. Overnight Russian drone attacks left about 280,000 households in the Dnipro and Kyiv regions without power, and Russia says it shot down 433 Ukrainian drones[^6]. The US also approved a $2.1 billion sale of 500 Patriot interceptor missiles, which the State Department says Canada, Germany and Norway are paying for[^6]. My read: a small, carefully policed deal worked here, which shows what is possible, but it does not show that a wider ceasefire is close.
topics.differences: Ukrainian volunteers and an unnamed source say Russia broke the agreed terms and pressured residents not to leave[^9][^7]. Russia's ombudswoman describes a humanitarian operation in which some people freely chose Russia[^8].

topics.heading: Early voting surges in the last weekend before the US midterm elections
topics.summary: Americans vote on Tuesday for all House seats and about a third of the Senate, and early voting is running well ahead of 2022. Polls favour Democrats nationally, but the Senate, where Republicans hold 53 of 100 seats, looks closer.[^10][^11]

lead.title: US midterms: 3 days to go – What latest polls say as early voting surges

alsoReported.title: Early voting jumps across Senate battlegrounds as millions more Americans vote ahead of Election Day
2026 elections live updates: the weekend before Election Day

article: With three days to go, about 43 million Americans had already voted, nearly 10 million more than at the same point in 2022, according to an AP count[^11][^10]. In Texas more than 6.3 million early votes were cast, up about 50%, and early voting also rose sharply in South Carolina, Maine, Kansas, Michigan and North Carolina[^11]. In states that report party, about 6.8 million Democrats and 5.2 million Republicans had voted early[^11]. Early voters are not a forecast, since many Republicans vote on the day itself.

Midterms are elections held halfway through a president's four-year term. A polling average cited by Al Jazeera puts Democrats ahead 51.4% to 43.2% on the "generic ballot", which asks which party people want in Congress[^10]. Kyle Kondik of the University of Virginia's Sabato's Crystal Ball says a Democratic takeover of the House is almost certain, while the Senate is "much more up in the air"[^10].

Republicans hold the Senate 53-47, so Democrats need a net gain of four seats[^11]. CBS News rates Alaska, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas as toss-ups[^12]. Polls show close races even in states Republicans usually win easily: one Emerson poll in Kansas has the Democrat ahead, and a New York Times/Siena poll in South Carolina is tied[^10][^12].

The background is the economy and the Iran war. Prices, especially fuel, have been central to the campaign, and on Friday Wall Street had its worst day since June as tech stocks fell[^22]. My read: if Democrats win the House, they could block or slow much of the president's agenda for the next two years, while a Senate win would also give them a say over judges and appointments. Results in close races may take days.
topics.differences: Early-vote totals differ by counter: AP counts about 43 million, while the University of Florida Election Lab counted about 44.8 million by Thursday evening[^11][^12]. Forecasters broadly agree on the House but differ on the Senate[^10][^12].

topics.heading: Herzog urges 'creative solutions' as Israel's coalition talks begin without a majority
topics.summary: Israel's president will start consultations on Wednesday after an election in which neither Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc nor Gadi Eisenkot's reached 61 of 120 seats. He urged leaders to avoid another election, while in Gaza the ceasefire remains fragile.[^13][^14][^15]

lead.title: Herzog Calls for 'Creative Solutions' Ahead of Wednesday Coalition Talks

alsoReported.title: Difficult talks ahead in Israel after Netanyahu's bloc loses majority
At least four Palestinians killed in Gaza as Israeli attacks continue

article: Israel's October 27 election left a deadlock: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc won 53 seats, former army chief Gadi Eisenkot's bloc 48, and Arab-led parties 19[^13][^14]. A government needs 61 of the Knesset's 120 seats. On Sunday President Isaac Herzog, who formally asks one leader to try to form a government, called for "creative solutions in order to prevent another election" and asked the bloc leaders to accept the results[^13]. His consultations with the parties start on Wednesday, November 4[^13].

The arithmetic is hard. Eisenkot could reach 61 only with support from Arab-led parties, but Avigdor Liberman, whose party has seven seats, calls them "supporters of terrorism" and appears to rule out such a partnership; AP says this makes an Eisenkot-led government nearly impossible[^14]. Netanyahu's Likud has spread unproven claims that the Arab parties "stole" the election; the election committee asked the Shin Bet security service to look into them, and Qatar called claims of its involvement "ridiculous and dangerous"[^14]. The new Knesset is expected to be sworn in on November 10, and if repeated attempts fail, Israel would vote again early next year[^14].

In Gaza, the October 2025 ceasefire holds only in name. Hospitals cited by Al Jazeera said at least four Palestinians were killed on Saturday, and Gaza's Health Ministry says about 1,580 people have been killed since the truce began[^15]. Talks on the next phase of the US plan are stuck: Hamas will not fully disarm until Israel withdraws, and Israel will not withdraw until Hamas disarms[^15].

My read: most observers expect little movement on Gaza until Israel has a government, and coalition talks could take weeks. Whoever leads will shape both the Gaza talks and Israel's role in the Iran war.
topics.differences: Likud says the Arab parties' result is suspect; police and the election authorities have said there is no evidence for the fraud claims[^14]. Gaza casualty figures come from the Health Ministry in Hamas-run Gaza, as cited by hospitals and Al Jazeera[^15].

topics.heading: UN nature summit ends in Yerevan with a 2030 plan but little new money
topics.summary: Countries at the UN biodiversity conference (COP17) in Armenia agreed a 'Yerevan Pathway' after the first global review found the world behind on 22 of 23 nature targets for 2030. Key money questions were pushed to 2028.[^16][^17]

lead.title: COP17: Key outcomes agreed at the UN biodiversity conference in Yerevan

alsoReported.title: Yerevan Pathway: COP17 ends with decisions on 50 agenda items
Global Summit Ends Without Securing Finance Commitments Needed to Protect Biodiversity

article: The UN's biodiversity conference, COP17, ended in the early hours of Saturday in Yerevan, Armenia, after a final session that lasted about 12 hours[^16]. Biodiversity means the variety of living things, from species to whole ecosystems. In 2022, countries agreed 23 targets to slow nature loss by 2030, including protecting 30% of land and sea, known as "30x30"[^18]. This meeting held the first global check of progress, and it found the world behind on 22 of the 23 targets[^16][^18].

Countries adopted decisions on about 50 agenda items and a "Yerevan Pathway" that sets priorities up to 2030[^17]. They agreed that a money mechanism will exist after 2030, but left its form to the next meeting, COP18 in Quito, Ecuador, in 2028[^16]. Richer countries missed their goal of providing $20 billion a year for nature by 2025[^16]. A fund meant to collect payments from companies that profit from genetic data from plants and animals had only about $10,565 pledged[^16].

Part of the problem is that governments still pay for activities that harm nature. Most countries (84%) missed a 2025 deadline to identify these "harmful subsidies"[^16]. A UN report cited by Common Dreams says the world spends $30 harming nature for every $1 it spends protecting it[^18].

Reactions split. The head of the UN biodiversity convention, Astrid Schomaker, said the real test is "what they change when they return home"[^17]. Conservation groups called the outcome too weak; one said "timidity will not save nature"[^17]. My read: nature loss gets less attention than climate change, but it affects food, water and health. The climate summit, COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, starts on November 9[^16].
topics.differences: Sources give different figures for new money pledged (about $1.8 billion versus about $2 billion) and for the size of harmful subsidies (up to $1.8 trillion a year versus $2.4 trillion)[^17][^18][^16]. Officials call the deal a pathway; environmental groups call it timid[^17].

topics.heading: Europe's central bank holds rates as Christine Lagarde says she will leave early
topics.summary: The European Central Bank kept its key rate at 2.5% after two hikes, as euro-area inflation runs near double its target. President Christine Lagarde will step down in February, about nine months early, a move critics call political.[^19][^20]

lead.title: ECB pauses rate hikes as Lagarde announces early exit

alsoReported.title: European Central Bank President Lagarde to step down early
Lagarde announces resignation after months of speculation

article: The European Central Bank (ECB), which sets interest rates for the 21 countries that use the euro, held its deposit rate at 2.5% on Thursday, after raising it twice in five months[^19]. Inflation in the euro area is close to double the ECB's 2% goal and could soon pass 4%, pushed up largely by energy prices since the Iran war began[^20][^19]. Markets expect another rate hike in December and about three more by the end of 2027[^21][^19].

The bigger news was a departure. Christine Lagarde said she will leave on February 7, 2027, about nine months before her term ends[^20][^21]. She said she leaves "with a sense of good work done and an ECB that is fit for the future"[^20]. Two other members of the bank's six-person executive board, Isabel Schnabel and Philip Lane, also leave next year[^19][^21].

Timing is the point of debate. Leaving early lets EU leaders pick her successor before France's presidential election in April 2027, in which far-right leader Marine Le Pen leads the polls[^20][^19]. Le Pen's camp called it "another insult in our direction", and a German member of the European Parliament warned it could damage trust in the bank's independence[^21][^20]. Supporters call it a responsible step[^20]. Reported front-runners to replace her are Klaas Knot of the Netherlands and Pablo Hernández de Cos of Spain[^19][^21].

Why it matters: central banks set the cost of borrowing, and inflation-fighting hikes hit mortgages, jobs and governments' debts. My read: Europe, the US and Canada all now face rising prices from the oil shock while growth slows, and a change at the top of the ECB adds one more uncertainty.
topics.differences: Lagarde's supporters say an early exit protects the ECB from a messy handover; critics, including Le Pen's party and some MEPs, say it looks political[^20][^21].
